newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austrian Air takes control of competitor Lauda.
newsitem.headline: Austrian Air takes control of competitor Lauda.

text.p: Austrian Airlines (AUA) said on Wednesday it would acquire a 36 percent voting stake in competitor Lauda Air, heralding a major shake-up in Austria's aviation industry.
"Austrian Airlines will take on 36 percent of the voting rights and strategic control of Lauda Air," supervisory board chief Rudolf Streicher told a news conference.
He said Lauda Air's founder and current majority owner, ex-racing driver Niki Lauda, would retain 30 percent of the voting rights and continue to serve as chief executive.

The annoucement came shortly after German flag carrier Lufthansa said it would cut its stake in Lauda Air to 20 percent from 39.7 percent and sell its holding to AUA. Some 15 percent of Lauda's shares will be widely held.

AUA said it had bought a total of 30 percent of Lauda shares from Lufthansa, which then replenished its holding to 20 percent through purchases from other investors. AUA also aquired an option to buy all remaining shares held by Niki Lauda at a fixed price until the year 2022.
Lufthansa said the sale would allow it to review possible cooperation deals with AUA and Lauda Air as well as regional carrier Tyrolean Airways, which is 42.85 percent owned by AUA.
"This is a good solution for the Austrian aviation industry," Streicher said, adding it would help the group to weather the increasingly tough competition in Europe's skies.
No financial details of the deal, which is subject to regulatory clearance, were released. AUA said it expected the link-up to be approved and to take effect on July 1st.
AUA, Lauda and Tyrolean have combined sales of about 20 billion schillings, and carry some 6.2 million passengers to more than 100 destinations on 77 aircraft.

According to the agreement, AUA will continue to concentrate on scheduled flights, while Lauda will retain its traditional niche as a charter carrier. Tyrolean will continue to concentrate on regional traffic.
"Our routes will not be changed, we will just make sure that there are no overlaps or parallel routes," AUA chief executive Herbert Bammer said.

Niki Lauda, who started up his airline in 1979 three years after crashing in his formula one racing car on Germany's Nuerburgring, said cooperating with his former arch-rival was in his best interests.
"For 18 years I worked against Austrian Air. But we don't stand a chance as competitors, we can't fly alone against the rest of the world," he told the news conference.
AUA said the Lauda deal would not affect its cooperation with Swissair, Delta Airlines, Belgium's Sabena, Singapor Airlines and All Nippon Airways.
